query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory alloy engineered to form a self-healing alumina (Al2O3) surface layer during exposure to molten aluminum at ~660°C will exhibit significantly reduced erosion compared to standard dipping equipment materials.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous refractory high‐temperature alloy (for example, one based on an AlCoCrFeNi-type composition or a similar high-entropy alloy) without preformed surface oxides.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy under simulated hot-dip aluminum plating conditions (≈660°C, prolonged contact with molten aluminum in a controlled atmosphere).
generation.conditions: Molten aluminum immersion at ~660°C for extended time periods that replicate typical service durations in dipping/plating operations.
generation.structural_mediator: The in-situ formation of a dense, adherent, and self-healing alumina layer on the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: During immersion, the alloy’s composition promotes rapid oxidation of surface aluminum (or aluminum-containing elements), forming a protective Al2O3 barrier that hinders further dissolution by molten aluminum and limits corrosion-driven material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in weight loss and degradation (erosion rate) compared to conventional materials (e.g., typical steels or alloys used in plating equipment), although the exact percentage improvement is uncertain.
generation.baseline: Standard dipping/plating equipment materials (e.g., common steels or low-alloy alloys) that lack a self-forming protective oxide and which suffer from rapid erosion when in contact with molten aluminum.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to be effective if the alumina layer remains continuous and intact; mechanical damage or compositional deviations that prevent adequate oxide formation may compromise performance.
generation.uncertainty: While the protective alumina mechanism is well documented in other high-temperature oxidation contexts, quantitative corrosion rate reductions under real hot-dip aluminum conditions and long-term cyclic thermal stresses remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare test coupons of the promising refractory alloy with controlled composition. Subject them to immersion in molten aluminum at approximately 660°C for a prolonged period (e.g., 100 hours) in an atmosphere replicating plating conditions. After exposure, perform microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS) to characterize surface oxide formation and measure weight loss to determine the corrosion rate. Compare these results to those obtained from coupons made of standard dipping materials.
measurements: Weight loss measurements pre- and post-exposure (to assess corrosion rate)
SEM/EDS surface analysis (to confirm the presence, continuity, and composition of the alumina layer)
Mechanical integrity tests (to evaluate any degradation in material properties)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the test alloy does not form a continuous, protective alumina layer or if its corrosion (erosion) rate under molten aluminum conditions is similar to or worse than that of conventional materials, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
